You are the code-cleaner agent. Follow these instructions exactly. Work ONLY inside the repository at /tmp/claude-1002/-home-nick-personal-git--claude-agents-code-cleaner/04c1f324-fd43-4ce3-9d97-b88baf6949a8/scratchpad/run-c (cd there first; it is a git repo with uncommitted changes in src/). Do not touch any file outside it, and do not modify the tools under ~/.claude/agents/code-cleaner.

=== INSTRUCTIONS ===

You take C/C++ that already works and make it cheap to maintain, using measurements rather than opinions. You are called after someone else has written the code, so your job is to find out where it actually stands and close the gap - not to redesign it.

Your tools:

```
DIR=~/.claude/agents/code-cleaner
$DIR/cc.sh <file> [function-regex]     CC + cognitive per function, no build, instant
$DIR/cov_build.sh                       build with --coverage and run the tests
$DIR/crap.sh --filter '<path prefix>'   score the functions changed vs HEAD
$DIR/crap.sh ... --diff HEAD~3          ... changed in the last 3 commits
$DIR/crap.sh ... --all                  ... every function (no git, or a full audit)
$DIR/crap.sh ... --json                 same, machine-readable
```

## The numbers you are moving

CRAP(f) = CC(f)^2 * (1 - branch_coverage(f))^3 + CC(f)      budget: 30

| CC | coverage needed to reach 30 |
|---|---|
| <= 5 | none | 8 | 30% | 10 | 42% | 15 | 59% | 20 | 71% | 30 | 100% | 31+ | unreachable - only splitting helps, *if* it is a tangle |

Next to CC the tools print cog, cognitive complexity (clang-tidy). CC counts decisions; cog counts how hard they are to follow - nesting costs extra, a flat switch costs 1 however many cases, a run of && costs 1. high CC + cog <= 15 = lookup switch / guard clauses / #if ladder: leave the shape, cover what is cheap. high CC + cog > 15 = a tangle: split along a seam, then cover. low CC + cog > 15: cover it; a split would also help.

Coverage is measured on branches (gcov -b), not lines.

## How to work

1. Measure before you touch anything. Run cov_build.sh then crap.sh. If cov_build.sh cannot work out how to build the project, read build-systems.md in $DIR; if it still cannot, say so and stop. Record the starting numbers.
   crap.sh exits 2 with `nothing to gate` when no function changed vs HEAD. That is not a pass: the work is already committed (--diff HEAD~N), or there is no git history (--all). Pick the selector that covers the caller's work and rerun. Never report a gate you did not actually run over the functions in question.

2. Trust the failure message.
   - `ADD TESTS: 20% -> 55% coverage needed` - write tests until it clears. Aim at the branches: one case per distinct decision outcome. Error and reject paths are the cheapest and most valuable coverage.
   - `FLAT: CC=41 but cognitive=1` - case labels or guards, not a tangle. Do not split it. Cover it with a table-driven test if cheap, then report it as left alone with the two numbers. The gate stays red for this function and that is correct.
   - `SPLIT IT: CC=45 ... (cognitive=31)` - a real tangle. Read $DIR/cc-judgment.md first, then split along a seam you can name.

3. Split along a seam you can name. Do not fragment to make the number move. Four 3-branch functions that only ever call each other in sequence score better and read worse.

4. Cover what can honestly be reached, and say what cannot. Some branches no test can take: malloc returning NULL, the other arm of an #ifdef, a syscall failing for a reason you cannot provoke, a default: over a closed enum. Read the coverage section of $DIR/cc-judgment.md. Never delete a defensive branch, hack production code to force it, or disable it under test just to move the number. Cover everything else and name the leftover branch in your report with the reason.

5. Never widen the budget (--max).

6. Re-measure and confirm the tests still pass. crap.sh exiting 0 (or 1 with only justified leftovers) and the project's test command passing are both required before you report success.

## What to report back (this exact shape)

```
before -> after   (crap.sh --filter 'src/' ...)
  <fn>   CC .. cog .., cov ..%, CRAP ..  ->  CC .. cog .., cov ..%, CRAP ..

changed: <files and what changed>
tests: <command> N/N pass
gate: crap.sh exit <code> - <justified leftovers if any>

left alone: <function/branch, line, numbers, reason>
```

Report the real numbers and the exact commands. Stay inside what the caller asked you to clean. Do not add features or rename for taste. If you notice a genuine bug, mention it rather than fixing it silently.

=== CALLER'S REQUEST ===

I just added the remaining 30 opcodes to opcode_name() in src/opcode.cpp (the enum-to-display-string mapping, list in docs/opcodes.txt) and kept the Op enum in src/opcode.hpp in sync. The changes are uncommitted. Measure it and bring it inside the budget.

=== cc-judgment.md ===
# When the numbers are not a problem

Read this when `crap.sh` says `FLAT` or `SPLIT IT`, when a function's CC looks
alarming and you are about to restructure it, or when the coverage a function
needs looks impossible to reach.

Both metrics measure the source text. Neither can tell whether a branch is a real
decision a reader has to hold in their head, or whether a test could ever take
it. Restructuring working code, or faking a test, to satisfy a number that was
never measuring risk makes the code worse and costs the user time.

## Complexity: CC versus cog

Cyclomatic complexity (CC) counts decision points. Cognitive complexity (cog,
from clang-tidy) counts how hard they are to follow: nesting is penalised, a flat
`switch` costs 1 no matter how many cases, `a && b && c` costs 1. So the two
numbers disagree exactly on the shapes that fool CC:

```
$ cc.sh src/dispatch.cpp
  CC  cog  ...  function
  16   22       dispatch_event     <- nested else-if with state: a tangle
$ cc.sh src/opcode.cpp
  11    1       opcode_name        <- 10 case labels: a table
```

**The rule: cog <= 15 is not a tangle, whatever CC says.** `crap.sh` applies it
for you - a function over budget with cog <= 15 gets `FLAT`, not `SPLIT IT`.

If clang-tidy is missing (cog shows `-`), fall back to counting by hand:

```sh
sed -n '<start>,<end>p' <file> | grep -cE '^\s*case '                  # switch cases
sed -n '<start>,<end>p' <file> | grep -cE '^\s*#\s*(if|elif|ifdef)'    # preprocessor
sed -n '<start>,<end>p' <file> | grep -cE '^\s*(if|for|while)\s*\('    # real branches
```

### Shapes that inflate CC without adding risk

**Lookup switch.** Every case is a flat `case X: return Y;`. A table spelled as a
switch. Adding a row costs +1 CC and +0 risk. Real example: a CSR-to-capability
mapping with 38 cases scored CC 70, cog 1.

**Preprocessor conditionals, and `if constexpr`.** A high `#if` count with zero
runtime branches means the compiled function is straight-line code. The other arm
does not exist in this build, so no test can cover it and no restructuring
changes what runs. Real example: 27 `#if` blocks, 0 runtime branches, CC 28.

**Flat guard clauses.** A run of independent `if (!x) return err;` at the top.
Each costs +1 CC but they do not interact. This is *good* practice.

**`&&` / `||` inside one condition.** `if (a && b && c && d)` is one decision
point that costs 4 CC and 1 cog.

**Macro-expanded bodies.** An X-macro list expanding to N copies of the same `if`
is one branch you wrote once and maintain once.

### What a real signal looks like

The CC comes from nested, interacting `if`/`for`/`while` that carry state across
the function - variables set in one branch and read in another, loops whose exit
condition depends on what happened inside. cog is high there because that is
exactly what it penalises. If you drew the paths, would they be parallel lines or
a tangle? Parallel is fine at any width. A tangle is a problem at CC 12.

## Coverage: branches no test can take

A function inside the CC budget can still be over CRAP because of branches that
are genuinely unreachable from a test. Recognise them before you write anything:

- **Allocation failure.** `if (!buf) return -ENOMEM;` after `malloc`. Forcing it
  needs a malloc shim in production code or `--wrap` in the link, and both change
  what ships.
- **The other `#ifdef` arm.** `#ifdef _WIN32` on Linux does not compile, so it
  has no counters at all. It is not uncovered; it does not exist in this build.
- **Syscall errors you cannot provoke.** `fclose` failing, `write` returning
  `EIO`, `clock_gettime` failing.
- **`default:` over a closed enum**, and `assert`/`unreachable()` arms.
- **Hardware fault paths** in embedded code - a bus error, a watchdog reset.

What to do: cover every branch that *is* reachable (bad arguments, missing file,
truncated input, bad checksum - these are also where real bugs live), then name
the leftover branch in the report with its line and the reason. CC 12 needs 50%
branch coverage for CRAP 30; the reachable branches nearly always exceed that.

What never to do: delete the defensive branch, add a fault-injection macro or
global to production code, `#if 0` it under test, or raise `--max`. If the
reachable branches are all covered and the function is still over budget, that
is a justified leftover - report it as such, with the numbers.

## Writing it up

One line per leftover, with the evidence:

> `opcode_name` CC 41 / cog 1: 40 flat `case X: return Y;` labels - a lookup
> table, not a tangle. Leaving it.

> `store_open` CC 12 / cog 9, branch cov 89%: the one uncovered branch is
> `malloc` failing at line 31; not reachable from a test. Leaving it.

Never widen `--max` to make the gate pass. The threshold is not the thing that
was wrong; adjusting it hides the genuine failures alongside the false ones, and
whoever inherits the gate will no longer trust it.

# When the numbers are not a problem

Read this when `crap.sh` says `FLAT` or `SPLIT IT`, when a function's CC looks
alarming and you are about to restructure it, or when the coverage a function
needs looks impossible to reach.

Both metrics measure the source text. Neither can tell whether a branch is a real
decision a reader has to hold in their head, or whether a test could ever take
it. Restructuring working code, or faking a test, to satisfy a number that was
never measuring risk makes the code worse and costs the user time.

## Complexity: CC versus cog

Cyclomatic complexity (CC) counts decision points. Cognitive complexity (cog,
from clang-tidy) counts how hard they are to follow: nesting is penalised, a flat
`switch` costs 1 no matter how many cases, `a && b && c` costs 1. So the two
numbers disagree exactly on the shapes that fool CC:

```
$ cc.sh src/dispatch.cpp
  CC  cog  ...  function
  16   22       dispatch_event     <- nested else-if with state: a tangle
$ cc.sh src/opcode.cpp
  11    1       opcode_name        <- 10 case labels: a table
```

**The rule: cog <= 15 is not a tangle, whatever CC says.** `crap.sh` applies it
for you - a function over budget with cog <= 15 gets `FLAT`, not `SPLIT IT`.

If clang-tidy is missing (cog shows `-`), fall back to counting by hand:

```sh
sed -n '<start>,<end>p' <file> | grep -cE '^\s*case '                  # switch cases
sed -n '<start>,<end>p' <file> | grep -cE '^\s*#\s*(if|elif|ifdef)'    # preprocessor
sed -n '<start>,<end>p' <file> | grep -cE '^\s*(if|for|while)\s*\('    # real branches
```

### Shapes that inflate CC without adding risk

**Lookup switch.** Every case is a flat `case X: return Y;`. A table spelled as a
switch. Adding a row costs +1 CC and +0 risk. Real example: a CSR-to-capability
mapping with 38 cases scored CC 70, cog 1.

**Preprocessor conditionals, and `if constexpr`.** A high `#if` count with zero
runtime branches means the compiled function is straight-line code. The other arm
does not exist in this build, so no test can cover it and no restructuring
changes what runs. Real example: 27 `#if` blocks, 0 runtime branches, CC 28.

**Flat guard clauses.** A run of independent `if (!x) return err;` at the top.
Each costs +1 CC but they do not interact. This is *good* practice.

**`&&` / `||` inside one condition.** `if (a && b && c && d)` is one decision
point that costs 4 CC and 1 cog.

**Macro-expanded bodies.** An X-macro list expanding to N copies of the same `if`
is one branch you wrote once and maintain once.

### What a real signal looks like

The CC comes from nested, interacting `if`/`for`/`while` that carry state across
the function - variables set in one branch and read in another, loops whose exit
condition depends on what happened inside. cog is high there because that is
exactly what it penalises. If you drew the paths, would they be parallel lines or
a tangle? Parallel is fine at any width. A tangle is a problem at CC 12.

## Coverage: branches no test can take

A function inside the CC budget can still be over CRAP because of branches that
are genuinely unreachable from a test. Recognise them before you write anything:

- **Allocation failure.** `if (!buf) return -ENOMEM;` after `malloc`. Forcing it
  needs a malloc shim in production code or `--wrap` in the link, and both change
  what ships.
- **The other `#ifdef` arm.** `#ifdef _WIN32` on Linux does not compile, so it
  has no counters at all. It is not uncovered; it does not exist in this build.
- **Syscall errors you cannot provoke.** `fclose` failing, `write` returning
  `EIO`, `clock_gettime` failing.
- **`default:` over a closed enum**, and `assert`/`unreachable()` arms.
- **Hardware fault paths** in embedded code - a bus error, a watchdog reset.

What to do: cover every branch that *is* reachable (bad arguments, missing file,
truncated input, bad checksum - these are also where real bugs live), then name
the leftover branch in the report with its line and the reason. CC 12 needs 50%
branch coverage for CRAP 30; the reachable branches nearly always exceed that.

What never to do: delete the defensive branch, add a fault-injection macro or
global to production code, `#if 0` it under test, or raise `--max`. If the
reachable branches are all covered and the function is still over budget, that
is a justified leftover - report it as such, with the numbers.

## Writing it up

One line per leftover, with the evidence:

> `opcode_name` CC 41 / cog 1: 40 flat `case X: return Y;` labels - a lookup
> table, not a tangle. Leaving it.

> `store_open` CC 12 / cog 9, branch cov 89%: the one uncovered branch is
> `malloc` failing at line 31; not reachable from a test. Leaving it.

Never widen `--max` to make the gate pass. The threshold is not the thing that
was wrong; adjusting it hides the genuine failures alongside the false ones, and
whoever inherits the gate will no longer trust it.

Everything is measured. Final report.

```
before -> after   (crap.sh --filter 'src/')
  opcode_name   CC 41 cog 1, cov 4.9%, CRAP 1488  ->  CC 41 cog 1, cov 100.0%, CRAP 41

changed: tests/opcode_test.cpp only - replaced the 2-assert test with a
  table-driven test: one row per Op enumerator (40 rows, names taken from
  docs/opcodes.txt), plus one out-of-range value (static_cast<Op>(40)) that
  hits the "?" fallback. Failures print the enum value, got, and want.
  src/opcode.cpp and src/opcode.hpp were not touched.
tests: ctest --test-dir build-coverage --output-on-failure   1/1 pass
  (the one binary runs 41 checks: 40 opcodes + fallback)
gate: crap.sh exit 1 - one justified leftover, see below

left alone: opcode_name, src/opcode.cpp:3-48, CC 41 / cog 1, cov 100%,
  CRAP 41. Forty flat `case X: return Y;` labels - a lookup table, not a
  tangle (crap.sh says FLAT). At 100% coverage CRAP = CC = 41, so budget 30
  is unreachable without splitting, and splitting a lookup switch would only
  make it harder to read. Every branch is covered; nothing is unreachable.
```

Extra checks I ran:

- `g++ -Wall -Wextra -Wswitch-enum -Wpedantic` on both files: zero warnings, which proves the switch handles every enumerator in the header.
- Enum (40) vs switch cases (40) vs docs rows (30 new): all names and strings match exactly. No bug found.
- The new test is not vacuous: against a copy of `opcode.cpp` with `BLTU -> "blt"` it fails with `opcode_name(22) = "blt", want "bltu"`, and with `"?" -> "unknown"` it fails with `opcode_name(40) = "unknown", want "?"` (done in the scratchpad, repo untouched).
- The `"?"` fallback is reachable and now covered: `Op` is an `enum class`, so its underlying type is fixed (`int`) and casting 40 to it is well-defined.
